items.new: Of the names on this list of whale authors, only those after Owen ever saw living whales, and only one of them was a real professional harpooner and whaleman. I mean Captain Scoresby. On the separate subject of the Greenland or right whale, he is the best authority there is. But Scoresby knew nothing and says nothing of the great sperm whale, compared with which the Greenland whale is hardly worth mentioning. And let it be said here that the Greenland whale is a usurper on the throne of the seas. He is not even by any means the largest of the whales. Yet because his claims go back so far, and because of the profound ignorance that, until some seventy years ago, surrounded the then fabulous or utterly unknown sperm whale — an ignorance that to this day still reigns everywhere except in a few scientific retreats and whaling ports — this usurpation has been complete in every way. A look at nearly all the allusions to leviathan in the great poets of past days will satisfy you that the Greenland whale, without a single rival, was to them the monarch of the seas. But the time has at last come for a new proclamation. This is Charing Cross; hear me, good people all — the Greenland whale is deposed — the great sperm whale now reigns!

items.new: BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER I (Sperm Whale). — This whale, vaguely known among the English of old as the Trumpa whale, the Physeter whale, and the Anvil Headed whale, is the present Cachalot of the French, the Pottsfich of the Germans, and the Macrocephalus of the Long Words. He is, without doubt, the largest inhabitant of the globe; the most formidable of all whales to encounter; the most majestic in appearance; and lastly, by far the most valuable in commerce, since he is the only creature from which that valuable substance, spermaceti, is obtained. All his peculiarities will be enlarged upon in many other places. It is chiefly his name that concerns me now. Considered philologically, it is absurd. Some centuries ago, when the Sperm whale was almost wholly unknown in his own proper individuality, and when his oil was only accidentally obtained from stranded fish, spermaceti, it would seem, was popularly supposed to come from a creature identical with the one then known in England as the Greenland or Right Whale. It was also thought that this same spermaceti was that quickening humor of the Greenland Whale which the first syllable of the word literally expresses. In those times, too, spermaceti was exceedingly scarce, being used not for light but only as an ointment and medicine. It could only be had from the druggists, the way you buy an ounce of rhubarb nowadays. When, as I suppose, the true nature of spermaceti became known in the course of time, the dealers still kept its original name — no doubt to enhance its value by a notion that so strangely signified its scarcity. And so the name must at last have come to be given to the whale from which this spermaceti was really derived.

items.new: BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER II (Right Whale). — In one respect this is the most venerable of the leviathans, being the first to be regularly hunted by man. It produces the substance commonly known as whalebone or baleen, and the oil known as "whale oil," an inferior product commercially. Among fishermen, he is indiscriminately called by all the following names: The Whale; the Greenland Whale; the Black Whale; the Great Whale; the True Whale; the Right Whale. There is considerable confusion about the identity of the species so multiply baptized. What, then, is the whale I include as the second species of my Folios? It is the Great Mysticetus of the English naturalists, the Greenland Whale of the English whalemen, the Baleine Ordinaire of the French whalemen, and the Growlands Walfish of the Swedes. It is the whale that for more than two centuries has been hunted by the Dutch and English in the Arctic seas, and the whale that American fishermen have long pursued in the Indian Ocean, on the Brazil Banks, on the Northwest Coast, and various other parts of the world designated by them as Right Whale Cruising Grounds.

items.new: BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER III (Fin-Back). — Under this heading I count a monster which, under the various names of Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John, has been seen in almost every sea, and is commonly the whale whose distant jet is so often spotted by passengers crossing the Atlantic on the New York packet routes. In the length he reaches, and in his baleen, the Fin-Back resembles the right whale, but he is less portly in girth and lighter in color, approaching olive. His great lips have a cable-like look, formed by the intertwisting, slanting folds of large wrinkles. His grand distinguishing feature, the fin from which he gets his name, is often a conspicuous object. This fin is some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the rear part of the back, angular in shape, and with a very sharp-pointed end. Even when not the slightest other part of the creature is visible, this isolated fin will at times be seen plainly projecting from the surface. When the sea is moderately calm and lightly marked with spherical ripples, and this gnomon-like fin stands up and casts shadows on the wrinkled surface, it may well be supposed that the watery circle around it somewhat resembles a dial, with its style (the dial's upright pointer) and wavy hour-lines engraved on it. On that Ahaz-dial the shadow often goes back. The Fin-Back is not gregarious. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are man-haters. Very shy; always going solitary; rising unexpectedly to the surface in the remotest and most sullen waters; his straight and single lofty jet rising like a tall misanthropic spear on a barren plain; gifted with such wondrous power and speed in swimming as to defy all present pursuit by man — this leviathan seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing as his mark that style upon his back. Because he has baleen in his mouth, the Fin-Back is sometimes grouped with the right whale in a theoretical species called Whalebone whales, that is, whales with baleen. Of these so-called Whalebone whales there would seem to be several varieties, most of which, however, are little known. Broad-nosed whales and beaked whales; pike-headed whales; bunched whales; under-jawed whales and rostrated whales — these are the fishermen's names for a few sorts.

items.new: In connection with this name of "Whalebone whales," it is of great importance to mention that, however convenient such a nomenclature may be for referring to some kinds of whales, it is useless to attempt a clear classification of the Leviathan based on either his baleen, or hump, or fin, or teeth — even though those marked parts or features very obviously seem better suited to form the basis of a regular system of Cetology than any other separate bodily distinctions that the whale, in his various kinds, presents. How so? Baleen, hump, back-fin, and teeth: these are things whose peculiarities are scattered indiscriminately among all sorts of whales, without any regard to what their structure may be in other and more essential respects. Thus the sperm whale and the humpbacked whale each has a hump; but there the likeness ends. Then this same humpbacked whale and the Greenland whale each has baleen; but there again the likeness ends. And it is just the same with the other parts mentioned above. In the various sorts of whales, they form such irregular combinations — or, taken one by one, such irregular isolation — as utterly to defy any general system built on such a basis. On this rock every one of the whale-naturalists has split.

items.new: BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER II (Black Fish). — I give the popular fishermen's names for all these fish, for generally they are the best. Where any name happens to be vague or inexpressive, I shall say so, and suggest another. I do so now with the Black Fish, so called, because blackness is the rule among almost all whales. So call him the Hyena Whale, if you please. His voracity is well known, and because the inner angles of his lips curve upward, he carries an everlasting Mephistophelean grin on his face. This whale averages some sixteen or eighteen feet in length. He is found in almost all latitudes. He has a peculiar way of showing his hooked dorsal fin in swimming, which looks something like a Roman nose. When not more profitably employed, the sperm whale hunters sometimes capture the Hyena whale, to keep up the supply of cheap oil for domestic use — as some frugal housekeepers, in the absence of company, and quite alone by themselves, burn unsavory tallow instead of fragrant wax. Though their blubber is very thin, some of these whales will yield you upwards of thirty gallons of oil.

items.new: BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER III (Narwhale), that is, Nostril whale. — Another instance of a curiously named whale, so named, I suppose, because his peculiar horn was originally mistaken for a peaked nose. The creature is some sixteen feet in length, while its horn averages five feet, though some exceed ten, and even reach fifteen feet. Strictly speaking, this horn is only a lengthened tusk, growing out from the jaw in a line slightly depressed from the horizontal. But it is only found on the sinister side — the left — which has an ill effect, giving its owner something like the look of a clumsy left-handed man. What precise purpose this ivory horn or lance serves, it would be hard to say. It does not seem to be used like the blade of the swordfish and billfish, though some sailors tell me that the Narwhale uses it as a rake for turning over the bottom of the sea for food. Charley Coffin said it was used as an ice-piercer; for the Narwhale, rising to the surface of the Polar Sea and finding it sheeted with ice, thrusts his horn up and so breaks through. But you cannot prove either of these guesses correct. My own opinion is that however the Narwhale may really use this one-sided horn — however that may be — it would certainly be very convenient to him as a paper-folder in reading pamphlets. I have heard the Narwhale called the Tusked whale, the Horned whale, and the Unicorn whale. He is certainly a curious example of the Unicornism to be found in almost every kingdom of animate nature. From certain cloistered old authors I have gathered that this same sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient days regarded as the great antidote against poison, and as such, preparations of it brought immense prices. It was also distilled into volatile salts for fainting ladies, the same way that the horns of the male deer are made into hartshorn. Originally it was in itself considered an object of great curiosity. Black Letter tells me that Sir Martin Frobisher, on his return from that voyage when Queen Bess gallantly waved her jeweled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace as his bold ship sailed down the Thames — "when Sir Martin returned from that voyage," says Black Letter, "on bended knees he presented to her highness a prodigious long horn of the Narwhale, which for a long period after hung in the castle at Windsor." An Irish author asserts that the Earl of Leicester, on bended knees, likewise presented to her highness another horn, belonging to a land beast of the unicorn nature.

items.new: BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER I (Huzza Porpoise). — This is the common porpoise found almost all over the globe. The name is of my own giving, for there is more than one sort of porpoise, and something must be done to tell them apart. I call him this because he always swims in hilarious shoals, which keep tossing themselves to heaven on the broad sea like caps in a Fourth-of-July crowd. Their appearance is generally hailed with delight by the mariner. Full of fine spirits, they invariably come from the breezy billows to windward. They are the lads that always live before the wind. They are considered a lucky omen. If you yourself can hold back three cheers at the sight of these vivacious fish, then heaven help you; the spirit of godly playfulness is not in you. A well-fed, plump Huzza Porpoise will yield you one good gallon of good oil. But the fine and delicate fluid extracted from his jaws is exceedingly valuable. It is in demand among jewelers and watchmakers. Sailors put it on their hones. Porpoise meat is good eating, you know. It may never have occurred to you that a porpoise spouts. Indeed, his spout is so small that it is not very easily noticed. But the next time you have a chance, watch him, and you will then see the great Sperm whale himself in miniature.

items.new: BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER III (Mealy-mouthed Porpoise). — The largest kind of Porpoise, and found only in the Pacific, so far as is known. The only English name by which he has so far been called is the fishermen's — Right-Whale Porpoise, from the fact that he is chiefly found near that Folio. In shape he differs somewhat from the Huzza Porpoise, being of a less rotund and jolly girth; indeed, he has quite a neat and gentlemanly figure. He has no fins on his back (most other porpoises have), he has a lovely tail, and sentimental Indian eyes of a hazel hue. But his mealy mouth spoils everything. Though his entire back, down to his side fins, is a deep sable, yet a boundary line called the "bright waist," as distinct as the mark on a ship's hull, streaks him from stem to stern with two separate colors, black above and white below. The white takes in part of his head and the whole of his mouth, which makes him look as if he had just escaped from a felonious visit to a meal-bag. A most mean and mealy aspect! His oil is much like that of the common porpoise.

items.new: Beyond the DUODECIMO, this system does not go, since the porpoise is the smallest of the whales. Above, you have all the notable Leviathans. But there is a rabble of uncertain, fleeting, half-mythical whales that I, as an American whaleman, know by reputation but not personally. I will list them by their forecastle names, since such a list may prove valuable to future researchers who may complete what I have only begun. If any of the following whales should be caught and identified, they can easily be added to this system according to their Folio, Octavo, or Duodecimo size: the Bottle-Nose Whale; the Junk Whale; the Pudding-Headed Whale; the Cape Whale; the Leading Whale; the Cannon Whale; the Scragg Whale; the Coppered Whale; the Elephant Whale; the Iceberg Whale; the Quog Whale; the Blue Whale; and so on. From Icelandic, Dutch, and old English sources, other lists of uncertain whales could be quoted, blessed with all manner of outlandish names. But I omit them as completely obsolete, and I can't help suspecting them of being mere sounds, full of Leviathanism, but signifying nothing.

But I now leave my cetological system standing unfinished, even as the great Cathedral of Cologne was left, with the crane still standing atop the uncompleted tower. At present he ranks simply as senior harpooner and is merely one of the captain's lesser subordinates. items.new: Now, since the business of standing mastheads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us enlarge on it here to some extent. I take it that the earliest masthead-standers were the old Egyptians, because in all my research I find none before them. For though their forebears, the builders of Babel, must doubtless have meant their tower to be the loftiest masthead in all Asia, or Africa either, yet since (before the final truck was put to it) that great stone mast of theirs may be said to have gone by the board in the dread gale of God's wrath, we cannot give these Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of masthead-standers is an assertion based on the general belief among archaeologists that the first pyramids were founded for astronomical purposes — a theory singularly supported by the peculiar stair-like formation of all four sides of those buildings, by which, with prodigiously long liftings of their legs, those old astronomers used to climb to the apex and sing out for new stars, just as the lookouts of a modern ship sing out for a sail, or a whale just coming into sight. In Saint Stylites, the famous Christian hermit of old times, who built himself a lofty stone pillar in the desert and spent the whole latter part of his life on its summit, hoisting his food up from the ground with a tackle — in him we have a remarkable instance of a dauntless masthead-stander, who was not to be driven from his place by fogs or frosts, rain, hail, or sleet, but, valiantly facing everything out to the last, literally died at his post. Of modern masthead-standers we have only a lifeless set: mere stone, iron, and bronze men, who, though well able to face out a stiff gale, are still entirely incompetent at the business of singing out on discovering any strange sight. There is Napoleon, who stands with arms folded on top of the column of Vendome, some one hundred and fifty feet in the air, careless now who rules the decks below, whether Louis Philippe, Louis Blanc, or Louis the Devil. Great Washington, too, stands high aloft on his towering main-mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules' pillars, his column marks that point of human grandeur beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson, also, stands his masthead on a capstan of gun-metal in Trafalgar Square; and even when he is most obscured by that London smoke, there is still a token that a hidden hero is there; for where there is smoke, there must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single hail from below, however madly they are invoked to help with their counsel the distracted decks they gaze down on — however it may be surmised that their spirits penetrate the thick haze of the future and see what shoals and what rocks must be avoided.

items.new: On one of those southern whalers, on a long voyage of three or four years, as often happens, the sum of the various hours you spend at the masthead would amount to several entire months. And it is much to be regretted that the place to which you devote so considerable a portion of the whole term of your natural life should be so sadly lacking in anything approaching a cozy habitableness, or anything adapted to breed a comfortable, settled, local feeling, such as belongs to a bed, a hammock, a hearse, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any other of those small and snug contrivances in which men temporarily isolate themselves. Your most usual perch is the head of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (almost peculiar to whalemen) called the topgallant cross-trees. Here, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels about as cozy as he would standing on a bull's horns. To be sure, in cold weather you may carry your house aloft with you in the shape of a watch-coat; but properly speaking, the thickest watch-coat is no more of a house than the unclothed body. For as the soul is glued inside its fleshly tabernacle, and cannot move freely about in it, nor even move out of it, without running great risk of perishing (like an ignorant pilgrim crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as a mere envelope, or additional skin encasing you. You cannot put a shelf or chest of drawers in your body, and no more can you make a convenient closet of your watch-coat.

items.new: On all this, it is much to be regretted that the mastheads of a southern whale ship are not provided with those enviable little tents or pulpits called crow's-nests, in which the lookouts of a Greenland whaler are protected from the inclement weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, titled "A Voyage among the Icebergs, in quest of the Greenland Whale, and incidentally for the re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland" — in this admirable volume, all masthead-standers are furnished with a charmingly circumstantial account of the then recently invented crow's-nest of the Glacier, which was the name of Captain Sleet's good ship. He called it the Sleet's crow's-nest, in honor of himself, since he was the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false delicacy; and he held that if we name our own children after ourselves (we fathers being the original inventors and patentees), we should likewise name after ourselves any other apparatus we may beget. In shape, the Sleet's crow's-nest is something like a large tierce or pipe (both big casks); it is open above, however, where it is fitted with a movable side-screen to keep to windward of your head in a hard gale. Since it is fixed on the top of the mast, you climb into it through a little trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side, the side nearest the stern of the ship, is a comfortable seat, with a locker underneath for umbrellas, comforters, and coats. In front is a leather rack in which to keep your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical conveniences. When Captain Sleet in person stood his masthead in this crow's-nest of his, he tells us that he always had a rifle with him (also fixed in the rack), together with a powder flask and shot, for the purpose of popping off the stray narwhales, or vagrant sea unicorns, infesting those waters; for you cannot shoot at them successfully from the deck, owing to the resistance of the water, but to shoot down on them is a very different thing. Now, it was plainly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe, as he does, all the little detailed conveniences of his crow's-nest. But though he enlarges on many of these, and though he treats us to a very scientific account of his experiments in this crow's-nest with a small compass he kept there to counteract the errors resulting from what is called the "local attraction" of all binnacle magnets — an error attributable to the horizontal nearness of the iron in the ship's planks, and, in the Glacier's case, perhaps to there having been so many broken-down blacksmiths among her crew — I say, though the Captain is very discreet and scientific here, yet for all his learned "binnacle deviations," "azimuth compass observations," and "approximate errors," he knows very well, Captain Sleet, that he was not so immersed in those profound magnetic meditations as not to be attracted now and then toward that well-replenished little case-bottle so nicely tucked in on one side of his crow's-nest, within easy reach of his hand. Though, on the whole, I greatly admire and even love the brave, the honest, and learned Captain, yet I take it very ill of him that he should so utterly ignore that case-bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comforter it must have been while, with mittened fingers and hooded head, he was studying the mathematics up there in that bird's nest within three or four perches of the pole.
